screens.body_html:
MODULE 04 · RESPONSIBLE

Who Does What

{{asset:char-omar-welcome}}Dr. Omar
screens.notes: Companion: Dr. Omar char-omar-welcome, L1 half-body bottom-right (alt: Dr. Omar, the course guide, welcoming the learner). Speaker: Omar. Brand kit draft in use ⚠ Draft — pending D11.
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: In this module, follow a patient through a visit and see how Operations and My Care contribute at different points. Notice how their work connects.

screens.title: Why it matters
screens.body_html:
“Right team, first time.”

A patient shouldn't have to tell their story twice.
screens.notes: Companion: Dr. Omar char-omar-explaining, L3 right column (media of the text_media layout). Speaker: Omar. Omar's three-desks story is used here once (companions.md §1).
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: A patient who has to repeat their story can lose confidence in the visit. The teams need to connect their work so the patient is guided smoothly from one stage to another. As you look at the journey, consider what a clear handoff feels like from the patient’s perspective.

screens.title: Make it yours
screens.prompt_html:
Which best describes your role?

We'll add tips for your work. Every scored activity is the same for everyone.

screens.title: Right team, first time
screens.body_html:
Can you get every patient to the right team, first time?

4 missions: 1 The patient journey · 2 Operations · 3 My Care · 4 Practice: right team, first time

Earn XP: +10 for each activity you get right · +5 for each quick check · +2 for each screen you explore. Ranks: Guide → Navigator → Coordinator → Journey Expert.

Patient trust (the dots at the top) goes up with each good decision and down with each risky one. Ask Noor or Dr. Omar for a hint before a big decision.

XP is just for you: it never counts towards your pass mark.
screens.notes: Gamification (tools/gamify.py, decision D18).

screens.title: Operations activities
screens.prompt_html: Operations runs the day. Open each activity.

items.title: Lab, Radiology and Pharmacy KPIs
items.body_html: Operations watches turnaround time (TAT) and waiting times for Lab, Radiology and Pharmacy.

items.title: Look and feel of the clinic
items.body_html: The clinic environment: clean, tidy and ready for patients.

items.title: Patient satisfaction
items.body_html: Operations tracks how patients rate their visit and acts on what they say.

items.title: End-to-end patient journey
items.body_html: From arrival to leaving, Operations keeps the visit flowing.

items.title: Support doctors and nurses
items.body_html: Operations helps clinicians with the non-clinical side of the visit so care runs on time.

items.title: Inquiries, on-spot complaints and recovery
items.body_html: Recovery: a patient waited 40 minutes; the PX officer apologises and fixes the next visit.

items.title: Daily operations
items.body_html: Running the clinic day: staffing the front of house and keeping services open.

screens.notes: 7 Operations activities from slide 2 (verified-facts register). The recovery example is from the card; the other one-line examples restate the activity and need SME confirmation (Director of Operations). Overlap with My Care on inquiries/complaints ⚠ Draft — pending B7. ops-img-activities is the planned shared line-icon set (one icon id until the 14 icons are split). No companion.
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: Operations supports the day-to-day environment, monitors KPIs, and helps recover service when something goes wrong. As you explore these activities, consider what each one means for the patient’s experience and for colleagues working across the clinic. Some issues may need attention from another team, so be clear about the part you own and when a handoff is needed.

screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: My Care continues the relationship beyond the visit through follow-ups, programmes, and referrals. As you open each section, consider how those activities connect with what happened during the appointment. A useful handoff gives the next colleague enough context to continue the patient’s care without asking them to start their story again. That continuity matters to the patient.

screens.title: Sort the work
screens.prompt_html: Place each of the 10 activities with the team that owns it: Operations or My Care.

items.text_html: On-spot complaint at reception ⚠ Draft — pending B7

targets.label_html: My Care — the relationship after the visit

feedback.correct_html:
Correct. Operations owns what happens in the clinic today: KPIs such as lab TAT, look and feel, the end-to-end journey, support for doctors and on-spot complaints. My Care owns the ongoing relationship: follow-up calls, insurance and medication follow-ups, programme bookings, telemedicine coordination and referral priority.

Overlap: both teams handle inquiries and complaints. A complaint made in the clinic right now goes to Operations; a service issue after the visit goes to My Care. Routing rule ⚠ Draft — pending B7.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not all 10 yet. Ask: is this happening in the clinic during today's visit (Operations), or is it part of the patient's care before or after the visit (My Care)? Inquiries and complaints sit in both lists — where and when the patient raises it decides the owner. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

screens.notes: Card answers follow the Phase 0 verified-facts lists (slides 2 and 5). The card asks for feedback on each card; edumints drag_drop has no per-item feedback, so the overlap explanation is in the screen feedback. Overlap items ⚠ Draft — pending B7. Keyboard pick-and-place is the player's default. No companion.
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: A request arrives during a busy shift. Read the details and decide how you would sort the work.

screens.title: Who do I call?
screens.intro_html:
{{asset:char-omar-avatar-neutral}}Dr. Omar · Family physician

Four patient requests. Route each one to the right team and role, first time. Pass with 3 of 4.

Routing answers ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

nodes.image_alt: A patient talks to a patient-experience officer at a clinic reception desk.
nodes.prompt_html: Request 1 of 4. At reception, a patient is upset: her lab result promised for today isn't ready. Who handles it?

choices.feedback_html:
Patient: “Thank you — someone is finally looking into it.”

✓ Better for the patient.

Yes. On-the-spot complaints and service recovery are Operations' job, led by the PX team on site. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

Patient: “The coordinator? I'm standing right here, upset, now.”

⚠ Risk for the patient.

My Care follows patients up after the visit. A complaint in the clinic right now needs the on-site PX team (Operations). ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

choices.text_html: Tell her to call back tomorrow
choices.feedback_html:
Patient: “So I have to come back and explain it all again?”

⚠ Risk for the patient.

Sending her away means she tells her story twice. The PX officer on site (Operations) owns recovery now. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

nodes.image_alt: A My Care coordinator on a phone follow-up call with a patient.
nodes.prompt_html: Request 2 of 4. A diabetic patient asks who will remind him about his 3-month review.

choices.text_html: My Care — his coordinator handles follow-ups and bookings
choices.feedback_html:
Patient: “Good, I'd forget otherwise.”

✓ Better for the patient.

Right. Follow-ups and programme bookings are My Care work; the My Care Coordinator keeps the review on track. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

choices.text_html: Operations — the PX officer at reception
choices.feedback_html:
Patient: “The front desk won't remember me in three months.”

⚠ Risk for the patient.

The PX officer looks after today's visit. A review in three months is part of the ongoing relationship: My Care. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

choices.text_html: He should set his own reminder
choices.feedback_html:
Patient: “I thought the clinic would remind me.”

⚠ Risk for the patient.

Follow-up reminders are a My Care service. Route him to his My Care Coordinator. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

nodes.image_alt: A staff member on an insurance call about a patient's medication approval.
nodes.prompt_html: Request 3 of 4. A patient's insurer rejected his monthly medication.

choices.text_html: My Care — insurance and medication follow-up
choices.feedback_html:
Patient: “So someone will follow up with the insurer for me?”

✓ Better for the patient.

Correct. Insurance and medication follow-ups are listed under My Care. The coordinator follows the rejection through. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

Patient: “The manager doesn't deal with my insurance, surely?”

⚠ Risk for the patient.

Operations runs the clinic day. Insurance and medication follow-ups belong to My Care. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

Patient: “The pharmacy told me to ask someone else.”

⚠ Risk for the patient.

The pharmacy dispenses, but following up an insurance rejection for monthly medication is a My Care task. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

nodes.image_alt: Patients waiting in a pharmacy queue in a clinic.
nodes.prompt_html: Request 4 of 4. A doctor reports the pharmacy queue is causing delays every afternoon.

choices.text_html: Operations — pharmacy KPIs and daily operations
choices.feedback_html:
Doctor: “Thanks — the afternoon queue is hurting my clinic times.”

✓ Better for the patient.

Yes. Pharmacy KPIs, the patient journey and support for doctors are Operations' job. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

Doctor: “This isn't about call quality, it's the queue.”

⚠ Risk for the patient.

The My Care QA leader checks the quality of My Care calls and service. A queue in the clinic is daily operations: Operations. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

Doctor: “I'm seeing patients — I can't run the pharmacy too.”

⚠ Risk for the patient.

Operations supports doctors and nurses so they can focus on care. Report the queue to Operations. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.

feedback.correct_html: Well routed. In-clinic issues today go to Operations; follow-ups, programmes and insurance go to My Care. ⚠ Draft — pending B7.
feedback.incorrect_html: Review each request: is it happening in the clinic now (Operations), or part of the patient's ongoing care (My Care)? Try again.

screens.title: Escalation
screens.prompt_html:
The PX officer can't resolve a complaint on the spot. Who is the next step?

Escalation line ⚠ Draft — pending B1.

options.feedback_html: Correct. On the draft Operations chart, PXOs report to the PX Managers at their site, so the site PX Manager is the next step. ⚠ Draft — pending B1.
The Director leads the whole structure. Escalate one step at a time: the PXO's own line manager comes first.
Coordinators handle follow-ups and bookings in My Care. An on-site complaint stays in the Operations line.
The QA leader checks the quality of My Care calls and service, not on-site complaint escalation.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. The next step is the site Patient Experience Manager — one level up the Operations line. ⚠ Draft — pending B1.
feedback.incorrect_html: Look again at the Operations structure: who sits directly above the PXOs at a site?

screens.notes: Correct answer from the card (site Patient Experience Manager, per B1) ⚠ Draft — pending B1. Distractors are roles shown on ops-011/ops-021. No companion over the question.
screens.narration_text: Dr. Omar: A concern needs escalation. Read the situation and decide what you would do next.

screens.title: Roles
screens.prompt_html: Match each role with what it does.

pairs.right_html: Quality of My Care calls and service

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Knowing what each role does tells you who to call: the PXO for the visit today, the coordinator for follow-ups, the onboarding leader for enrolment, the Operations Sr. Manager for the clinic day and the QA leader for My Care service quality.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not all five. Think about where each role works: on site during the visit (Operations) or with the patient over time (My Care).

screens.notes: Pairs verbatim from the card. Role titles follow the draft charts ⚠ Draft — pending B1 / B2. No companion.

  • My Care carries the relationship: follow-ups, programmes, insurance, referrals.
  • Route by where and when: in the clinic now, or the patient's ongoing care.
  • Escalate one step at a time, by role.
